transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-22
Time: 15:00 - 16:02 UTC
Duration: 62 min
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Arjun (Redwood SE), Mira (Redwood CSM), Samir (Pegasus VP Eng), Dana (Pegasus SRE), Olivia (Pegasus Security)

Summary: quick postmortem of 2027-10-18 production incident where Pegasus saw elevated tail latency and 503s during a large nightly batch; review mitigations, long-term reliability fixes (dedicated GPU pools, KV cache warmup, autoscale tuning), and next steps to run benchmarks and share security artifacts.

Topics: Incident timeline, Root cause hypotheses, Short-term mitigations, Dedicated/private deployment options, Security & compliance questions, Benchmarks and pilot plan, Action items and owner recap

[00:00] Lena: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to run through the postmortem from monday night, go over what happened, what we did, and next steps. arjun do you want to start with a quick timeline?
[00:18] Arjun: yeah, I'll take it. so at ~02:12 UTC on 2027-10-18 we started seeing increased 95th/99th latency for text-generation endpoints. by 02:20 error rates spiked to about 6% 503s, mostly on a subset of nodes handling long-context requests. initial mitigation was to fallback to a smaller model variant and enable prefix cache flush which reduced errors by 80% over 15 minutes.
[00:46] Samir: couple questions off the bat — was this more of a model-level memory pressure issue or a serving runtime kernel issue? our ops saw OOM-ish signals but not full container terminations.
[01:02] Arjun: good question. our current hypothesis is a combination: sustained KV-cache growth for long sessions plus a regression in a recent kernel selector that caused higher memory residency on certain GPUs. not a pure model OOM, more fragmentation + slower GC path. we saw per-GPU usable memory drop below expected for those instances.
[01:25] Dana: i remember we had a really heavy overnight batch of embeddings + long chat sessions. our traffic profile peaked around 1.6x normal for about 45 minutes during the window. could that have pushed cache to blow past the warmup thresholds?
[01:37] Arjun: yeah, the cache policy assumed a steady-state distribution. the burst mixed long prefix reuse and many unique sessions which caused KV growth. we should improve cache eviction heuristics for mixed workloads.
[01:51] Mira: short-term we applied model fallback and restarted a few GPU workers which stabilized things. longer term the dedicated pool autoscale thresholds need adjusting and kernel selector rollback is being evaluated.
[02:05] Olivia: security — did any of the restarts cause loss of audit logs or incomplete request traces? we rely on those for incident forensics.
[02:14] Arjun: we kept trace ingestion but there were some gaps at the per-worker level during restarts; centralized audit log stream was intact. we'll attach the partial logs to the RCA.
[02:25] Samir: okay, what are the concrete next mitigations we recommend so this doesn't repeat?
[02:32] Lena: i'll let arjun list the technical fixes and then we'll cover ops/process and security items.
[02:36] Arjun: short-term: 1) pin model variants for night-batch windows and add automatic fallback to lighter quantized variant; 2) adjust KV cache eviction to prioritize TTL + LRU hybrid during burst windows; 3) rollback kernel-selector change introduced 10/10 and push a canary to 10% before full rollout. mid-term: dedicated reserved GPU pool for Pegasus with tuned autoscale (min headroom 20%); longer-term: instrument memory defragmentation metrics and implement proactive cache pre-warming for scheduled heavy jobs.
[03:10] Dana: how quickly can we get the kernel-selector rollback? we had the change staged in the last deploy batch.
[03:18] Arjun: it's ready, we can rollback in <24 hours but want to run a short regression run in staging first. plan is rollback to previous kernel path and then run the regression test; timeline 2027-10-23.
[03:30] Samir: about dedicated pool — what's the expected latency improvement and cost delta? our finance team will ask.
[03:38] Mira: from our prior benchmarks a dedicated pool tuned for your workload reduces tail latency by ~30-45% depending on sequence length and eliminates noisy neighbor variance. cost is roughly 1.6-2.2x of mixed-hosting for the same provisioned QPS but predictable — we can run a pilot and show the unit economics.
[03:58] Olivia: on compliance, we need to see KMS integration docs and SOC2 artifact for log retention and key rotation. also confirm that on-prem/private deployment doesn't ship PII to Redwood's hosted telemetry.
[04:14] Lena: yes we'll share the SOC2 pack and KMS integration notes. for private deployments, telemetry is opt-in and we can provide audited hooks that keep request content local; we'll include exact config snippets.
[04:28] Samir: returning to root cause — are we confident this isn't a regression in our client usage patterns? we did roll out longer multi-turn sessions last month.
[04:38] Arjun: we looked at request traces and yes there is a higher proportion of long-run sessions; still that alone wouldn't have caused the fragmentation without the kernel selector change. it's the combination that tipped the memory behavior past the safety margin.
[04:53] Dana: any immediate config change we should make on our side? throttle the embedding bulk or move heavy batch to a quieter window?
[05:01] Samir: we can shift the embedding job earlier in the night by 3 hours, but we'd prefer Redwood handle mixed workload safely.
[05:10] Mira: that's fair — our recommended path is pilot dedicated pool with scheduling controls for heavy batch jobs plus canary rollback.
[05:18] Arjun: also adding a runtime health probe that monitors per-GPU memory fragmentation and triggers autoscaler or cache eviction earlier.
[05:28] Lena: okay let's cover the benchmark plan: we'll run a 2-hour stress window that simulates your observed pattern (1.6x burst with mixed long sessions + embeddings). we propose next monday 2027-10-25 02:00-04:00 UTC — does that work for pegasus?
[05:44] Samir: that's fine, we'll get Dana and the ops team there.
[05:49] Dana: yes we'll be available. we'll also share the traffic CSV.
[05:54] Lena: perfect. security items — olivia, what do you need from us to close the compliance questions?
[06:02] Olivia: SOC2 evidence, KMS integration steps, retention and redact controls, and a short note on telemetry opt-in for private deploys. also confirm RBAC audit logging is available per-user.
[06:15] Lena: we'll send those; expect SOC2 pdf + KMS guide + RBAC audit sample by 2027-10-23.
[06:22] Arjun: quick note on monitoring: we'll add a dashboard tile for cache size, fragmentation metric, and per-GPU eviction counts so both teams can watch during the pilot.
[06:35] Samir: great. can you also attach the partial logs you mentioned earlier so our forensic team can cross-check?
[06:40] Arjun: yes, we'll attach request/response pairs and kernel traces; note some worker-level traces are partial due to restarts.
[06:47] Mira: i'll schedule the benchmark and send calendar invites; arjun will own the in-test run and lena will handle customer comms.
[06:56] Samir: timeline recap please?
[07:00] Lena: sure — action items: arjun share logs and kernel traces 10/25, arjun run kernel-selector rollback/regression in staging by 10/23, mira schedule benchmark by 10/24 and run on 10/25, lena send SOC2/KMS docs by 10/23, pegasus (dana) provide traffic CSV by 10/26, olivia confirm retention rules by 10/26.
[07:26] Samir: sounds good. any other risks we're not covering?
[07:30] Arjun: one small risk — if your traffic profile changes to even longer lived KV usage we'll need a longer-term defragmentation path built into the runtime which is an engineering project into next quarter. we'll flag it as roadmap work.
[07:44] Dana: understood. thanks everyone.
[07:47] Lena: thanks all, we'll follow up with notes and docs. end.
